Stokes | Rossolis septentrionalis | Scop. }} }} '''''Drosera rotundifolia''''', the '''round-leaved sundew''',{{cite web | title=Round-leaved Sundew ''Drosera rotundifolia'' L. | website=PlantAtlas | url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.z3 | access-date=2025-08-27}} '''roundleaf sundew''', or '''common sundew''', is a [[species]] of [[carnivorous plant|carnivorous]] [[flowering plant]] that grows in [[bog]]s, [[marsh]]es and [[fen]]s. One of the most widespread sundew species, it has a [[circumboreal]] distribution, being found in almost all of [[Europe]], all of [[Siberia]], large parts of [[North America]], [[Korea]] and [[Japan]] but is also found as far south as eastern [[China]], the [[Philippines]], and into the Southern Hemisphere in [[New Guinea]]. ==Description== [[Image:Rotundifolia leaf morphology.jpg|thumb|left|65px|A ''Drosera rotundifolia'' leaf on a 1 mm grid]] The [[leaf|leaves]] of the common sundew are arranged in a basal [[rosette (botany)|rosette]]. The narrow, hairy, {{convert|1.3|to|5.0|cm|in|1|adj=on}} long [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]] support {{convert|4|to|10|mm|in|1|adj=on}} round laminae. The upper surface of the [[Leaf|lamina]] is densely covered with red glandular hairs that secrete a sticky [[mucilage]]. A typical plant has a diameter of around {{convert|3|to|5|cm|in}}, with a {{convert|5|to|25|cm|in|0|adj=on}} tall [[inflorescence]]. The [[flower]]s grow on one side of a single slender, hairless stalk that emanates from the centre of the leaf rosette. White or pink in colour, the five-petalled flowers produce light brown, slender, tapered [[seed]]s {{convert|1.0|to|1.5|mm|in|2|adj=on}}.{{cite book | author=Regents of the University of California | title=The Jepson Manual: Higher Plants of California | publisher=University of California Press | location=Berkeley, California | year=1993 | url=http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?3427,3428,3430 }} In winter, ''D. rotundifolia'' produces a [[Hibernaculum (botany)|hibernaculum]] to survive cold conditions. This consists of a bud of tightly curled leaves at ground level. ==Carnivory== [[Image:Drosera rotundifolia ne2.jpg|thumb|220px|right|''D. rotundifolia'' with the remains of a butterfly]] The plant feeds on [[insect]]s, which are attracted to the glistening drops of mucilage, loaded with a sugary substance, covering its leaves. It has evolved this [[carnivorous]] behaviour in response to its habitat, which is usually poor in nutrients or is so acidic that nutrient availability is severely decreased. The plant uses [[enzymes]] to dissolve the insects which become stuck to the glandular [[tentacles]], and extract [[ammonia]] from proteins and other nutrients from their bodies.{{cite web|title=Drosera rotundifolia: Round-leafed Sundew |url=https://msu.edu/course/plb/423/Species_Accounts/Drosera/Species%20Account.htm |website=msu.edu |access-date=22 May 2017 |language=en}} The ammonia replaces the nitrogen that other plants absorb from the soil, and plants that are placed in a high-nitrogen environment rely less upon nitrogen from captured insects.{{cite journal|last1=Millett|first1=J.|last2=Svensson|first2=B. M.|last3=Newton|first3=J.|last4=Rydin|first4=H.|title=Reliance on prey-derived nitrogen by the carnivorous plant ''Drosera rotundifolia'' decreases with increasing nitrogen deposition |journal=New Phytologist |date=July 2012 |volume=195 |issue=1 |pages=182–188 |doi=10.1111/j.1469-8137.2012.04139.x |pmid=22506640 |url=http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/store/10.1111/j.1469-8137.2012.04139.x/asset/j.1469-8137.2012.04139.x.pdf;jsessionid=EAEC77B6389F097754A8FDF63467113A.f01t04?v=1&t=j306yepb&s=cfa652331b868c845ef538b60f2a1df1794f3f6c |access-date=22 May 2017 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2012NewPh.195..182M }} It has been assumed that insects were also attracted to the bright red colour of the common sundew, but studies using artificial traps have suggested that colour does not affect prey attraction.{{cite journal|last1=Foot|first1=G.|last2=Rice|first2=S. P.|last3=Millett|first3=J.|title=Red trap colour of the carnivorous plant ''Drosera rotundifolia'' does not serve a prey attraction or camouflage function|journal=Biology Letters|date=16 April 2014|volume=10|issue=4|article-number=20131024|doi=10.1098/rsbl.2013.1024|pmid=24740904|pmc=4013691}} In newly discovered climates with the plant but do not have the food associated with the requirements for growth, new studies have been conducted to determine how they are able to grow.  In one study, the carnivory of ''Drosera rotundifolia'' was tested against growing conditions where the plant's insect prey was not sufficient to promote proper growth.  The study tested the plant's ability to grow with limited prey but increased inorganic nutrients within the soil.  The results revealed the ability of the plant to use nutrients underground instead of relying on carnivory, suggesting the plant is able to adapt according to the availability of nutrients.{{Cite journal |last1=Thorén |first1=L. Magnus |last2=Tuomi |first2=Juha |last3=Kämäräinen |first3=Terttu |last4=Laine |first4=Kari |date=2003–2008 |title=Resource availability affects investment in carnivory in ''Drosera rotundifolia'' |journal=New Phytologist |language=en |volume=159 |issue=2 |pages=507–511 |doi=10.1046/j.1469-8137.2003.00816.x |pmid=33873350 |issn=0028-646X|doi-access=free |bibcode=2003NewPh.159..507T }} ==Distribution== [[Image:Drosera rotundifolia Distribution Map.png|thumb|left|250px|Roundleaf sundew range (red = common; pink = scattered)]] In [[North America]], the common sundew is found in all parts of [[Canada]] except the [[Canadian Prairies]] and the [[tundra]] regions, southern [[Alaska]], the [[Pacific Northwest]], and along the [[Appalachian Mountains]] south to [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]] and [[Louisiana]]. In the western United States, roundleaf sundew is found in mountain fens as far south as the Sierra Nevada of California and in a disjunct cluster of fen occurrences in the Rocky Mountains of Colorado.{{cite journal|last1=Wolf|first1=Evan|last2=Gage|first2=Edward|last3=Cooper|first3=David|title=''Drosera rotundifolia'' L. (roundleaf sundew): A Technical Conservation Assessment|journal=USDA Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Region, Species Conservation Project|date=2006-06-26|url=http://www.fs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_DOCUMENTS/stelprdb5206848.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170227191301/https://www.fs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_DOCUMENTS/stelprdb5206848.pdf|archive-date=27 February 2017}} In the eastern United States, the sundew plant is found in parts stretching from Nova Scotia down the coast into Georgia.  In addition to Georgia, plants are now being seen in Alabama and Mississippi.  West of the Mississippi River, plants are located along the Pacific coast from Alaska down the coast to California, with new plants detected in Iowa, Minnesota and in two recently recorded sites in Gunnison County, Colorado and Bottineau County, North Dakota.{{Cite web |title=''Drosera rotundifolia'' |url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/database/feis/plants/forb/drorot/all.html |access-date=2022-12-03 |website=www.fs.usda.gov}} It is found in much of [[Europe]], including the [[British Isles]], most of [[France]], the [[Benelux]] nations, [[Germany]], [[Denmark]], [[Switzerland]], [[Czech Republic]], [[Poland]], [[Belarus]], the [[Baltic countries]], [[Sweden]] and [[Finland]], as well as northern portions of [[Italy]], [[Portugal]], [[Spain]], [[Romania]], mountain regions of [[Bulgaria]] and in [[Iceland]] and southern regions of [[Norway]] and [[Greenland]]. It is infrequent in [[Austria]] and [[Hungary]], and some populations are scattered around the [[Balkans]].{{Citation needed|date=May 2025}} In [[Great Britain|Britain]], this is the most common sundew species, found widely in the west and north, from [[Exmoor]], [[Dartmoor]], [[Sedgemoor]], the [[Lake District]], [[Shropshire]], [[Pennines]] and throughout [[Scotland]]; conversely it is rare and scattered in the [[Midlands]] and eastern England. It is usually found in bogs, marshes and in hollows or [[corries]] on the sides of mountains. It is the county flower of Shropshire.{{Cite web|title = Round-leaved sundew {{!}} Plant & fungi species {{!}} Wild plants|url = http://www.plantlife.org.uk/wild_plants/plant_species/round-leaved_sundew/|website = www.plantlife.org.uk|access-date = 2016-01-03|archive-date = 2010-10-06|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20101006064437/http://www.plantlife.org.uk/wild_plants/plant_species/round-leaved_sundew/}} It is also common in [[Ireland]]. In [[Asia]], it is found across [[Siberia]] and [[Japan]], as well as parts of [[Turkey]], the [[Caucasus]] region, the [[Kamchatka Peninsula]], southern parts of [[Korea]], and northeastern and eastern [[China]]. Populations can also be found on the islands of [[New Guinea]] and [[Mindanao]].{{cite journal |last1=Coritico |first1=Fulgent |last2=Fleischmann |first2=Andreas |title=The first record of the boreal bog species ''Drosera rotundifolia'' (Droseraceae) from the Philippines, and a key to the Philippine sundews |journal=Blumea |date=January 2016 |volume=61 |issue=1 |pages=24–28 |doi=10.3767/000651916X691330 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2016Blume..61...24C |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/303734731 |access-date=10 December 2021}} ==Habitat== [[Image:Drosera rotundifolia habitat.jpg|thumb|right|220px|''D. rotundifolia'' growing in [[sphagnum moss]] along with [[sedges]] and ''[[Equisetum]]'']] The common sundew thrives in wetlands such as [[marsh]]es and [[fen]]s.C.Michael Hogan. 2011. [http://www.eoearth.org/article/Drosera_rotundifolia?topic=49540 ''Drosera rotundifolia''. Encyclopedia of Earth. Eds. M.McGinley & C.J.Cleveland. National Council for Science and the Environment. Washington DC] It is also found in wet stands of [[black spruce]], ''[[Sphagnum]]'' bogs, silty and boggy shorelines and wet sands. It prefers open, sunny or partly sunny habitats. ==Conservation== The round-leaved sundew is classified as Least Concern in the IUCN red list. In [[North America]], it is considered [[endangered]] in the [[United States|US]] states of [[Illinois]] and [[Iowa]], exploitably vulnerable in [[New York state|New York]], and threatened in [[Tennessee]].{{Cite PLANTS|symbol=DRRO|taxon=Drosera rotundifolia}} The species is ranked S2, imperiled, in the state of Colorado.{{cite web|title=USFS species evaluation|url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_DOCUMENTS/stelprdb5261743.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170302000019/https://www.fs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_DOCUMENTS/stelprdb5261743.pdf|archive-date=2 March 2017}} ==Cultivation== ''D. rotundifolia'' is one of the temperate species of ''Drosera'' cultivated by growers interested in carnivorous plants. To be grown successfully, plants of the wild species must be given a substantial period of winter dormancy during which they form [[Hibernaculum (botany)|hibernacula]]. The [[cultivar]] ''D. rotundifolia'' 'Charles Darwin' can be grown more successfully without a period of dormancy.{{cite web |first=John |last=Brittnacher |title=Growing cold temperate ''Drosera'' |publisher=International Carnivorous Plant Society |url=http://www.carnivorousplants.org/howto/GrowingGuides/DroseraColdTemperate.php |access-date=2013-06-19 }} ==Medicinal properties== [[File:Drosera rotundifolia Brown's Lake Bog.jpg|thumb|''Drosera rotundifolia'' at [[Brown's Lake Bog]], [[Ohio]].]] According to D.H. Paper, ''et al.'',{{cite journal |last1=Paper |first1=D.H. |last2=Karall |first2=E. |last3=Kremser |first3=M. |last4=Krenn |first4=L. |title=Comparison of the antiinflammatory effects of ''Drosera rotundifolia'' and ''Drosera madagascariensis'' in the HET-CAM assay |journal=Phytotherapy Research |volume=19 |issue=4 |pages=323–6 |date=April 2005 |pmid=16041727 |doi=10.1002/ptr.1666|s2cid=20405232 }} ''Drosera rotundifolia'' plant extracts show great efficacy as an [[anti-inflammatory]] and [[antispasmodic]], more so than ''[[Drosera madagascariensis|D. madagascariensis]]'', as a result of the [[flavonoid]]s such as [[hyperoside]], [[quercetin]] and [[isoquercetin]], but not the [[naphthoquinone]]s present in the extracts. The flavonoids are thought{{cite journal |vauthors=Krenn L, Beyer G, Pertz HH |title=In vitro antispasmodic and anti-inflammatory effects of ''Drosera rotundifolia'' |journal=Arzneimittelforschung |volume=54 |issue=7 |pages=402–5 |year=2004 |pmid=15344845 |doi=10.1055/s-0031-1296991|display-authors=etal}} to affect the M3 [[muscarinic receptor]]s in [[smooth muscle]], causing the antispasmodic effects. [[Ellagic acid]] in ''D. rotundifolia'' extracts has also been shown to have anti[[angiogenesis|angiogenic]] effects.{{Citation needed|date=May 2025}} ==Notes== {{Reflist}} ==References== *{{cite book |author1=Karen Legasy |author2=Shayna LaBelle-Beadman |author3=Brenda Chambers. |title=Forest Plants of Northeastern Ontario |publisher=Lone Pine Publishing |location=Ontario |year=1995 }} *{{in lang|sv}} [http://linnaeus.nrm.se/flora/di/drosera/drose/drosrot.html ''Den virtuella floran - Rundsileshår''].
